newsitem.title: ISRAEL: West Bank and Gaza quiet after Washington summit.
newsitem.headline: West Bank and Gaza quiet after Washington summit.

text.p: Palestinians threw stones at Israeli troops in Hebron on Thursday but most parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip were quiet a day after a Washington peace summit which the PLO called a failure.

Demonstrators clashed briefly with Israeli soldiers as authorities temporarily lifted a curfew in Hebron -- a focus of contention between the two sides -- to allow residents to stock up on food and other supplies, witnesses said.
On nearby hills, Israeli tanks pointed their barrels at Palestinian towns below and soldiers braced for any renewal of violence which has killed 73 people since last week.

"I have no doubt that the appearance of armoured forces in the area made a meaningful contribution to our deterrence and if anyone dares (to provoke Israel) he will experience the fire power of Israel's armour," Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said in remarks on Israeli radio.

Israel hailed the Washington summit which brought together Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat for only the second time since the Israeli leader was elected in May.
But Palestinians said it had achieved nothing.
"The summit has failed because of Israeli intransigence," Hasan Asfour, a PLO negotiator, told Reuters.
Mustafa Natsheh, the Palestinian mayor of Hebron where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians, said the peace process was on the verge of collapse.
"Unless international and Arab public opinion and Israeli peace groups move, the area will not witness any calm and the cycle of violence will return anew," he said.
Palestinians failed to get Israel to commit to a date for a troop redeployment in Hebron, a partial pullout agreed by the previous Labour-led government in a deal reached a year ago.
Instead, the two sides agreed to intensify talks starting on Sunday with mediation efforts by U.S. peace coordinator Dennis Ross.
"The results of the summit are a great success from the point of view of the government of Israel," Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh told Israel Radio from Washington.
While Palestinians were united in disappointment, Israelis were divided over what their government termed a victory.

"I think that Bibi Netanyahu gambled in Washington with the fate of the state...no one can know right now how many people will have to pay with their lives for this wild gamble," Yossi Sarid, member of parliament and head of the leftist Meretz party, told Israel's army radio, using Netanyahu's nickname.

Pinchas Wallerstein, leader of the 130,000 Jews settled amid nearly two million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, said: "I'm very glad about the prime minister's firm position but on the other hand I'm worried about the Palestinian reaction."
In the West Bank on Wednesday, Israeli troops, enforcing travel restrictions on Palestinians, killed one Arab and wounded five, the Israeli army and Palestinians said.

The violence raised the death toll to 58 Palestinians and 15 Israelis since last week when Israel's opening of a second entrance to a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem sparked widespread gun battles and clashes.

President Bill Clinton told a White House news conference after the two-day summit that Arafat and Netanyahu failed to resolve their differences. He said the Middle East peace process was still in crisis.
Clinton said the two sides had agreed to resume immediate peace talks focusing on an Israeli pullback from Hebron, far less than Arafat's demand for immediate redeployment.

Faisal al-Husseini, senior PLO representative in Jerusalem, told Israel Radio: "In this situation tomorrow (Thursday) there is a possibility that there will be nothing but there is a possibility that there will be another explosion."
He added: "I was never as pessimistic as I am today."
